They doubled down on the API after the first big client.
words.mission: Say what your team should double down on, and what to drop.

words.trap: Not 'achever' (to finish) — for that say finish or complete. Achieve means reach a goal.
words.definition: to succeed in reaching a goal after effort.
examples: We achieved the latency target a month early.
What do we want to achieve by the end of the year?
words.mission: Say what you want to achieve this quarter — not 'finish'.

words.definition: a very ambitious project that is unlikely to succeed but would change everything if it did.
examples: Real-time translation is our moonshot for next year.
One moonshot per year, the rest must pay the bills.
words.mission: Name one moonshot your team could try.

words.definition: the one goal or measure that guides every decision.
examples: Our north star is weekly active teams, not sign-ups.
When in doubt, check the decision against the north star.
words.mission: Say what the north star of your product is, in five words.

words.definition: to decide not to continue a plan for now, perhaps forever.
examples: We shelved the redesign to focus on reliability.
The idea was shelved, not killed.
words.mission: Say what you would shelve to make room for the priority.

words.definition: being planned or developed, but not finished.
examples: A self-service portal is in the works.
Several fixes are in the works for the next release.
words.mission: Say what is in the works without promising a date.

words.definition: what can be won or lost in a situation; how much it matters.
examples: The stakes are high: this client is a third of revenue.
Low stakes — it's an internal tool.
words.mission: Say how high the stakes are for one decision, and why.

words.definition: to decide what to do as things happen, rather than planning in advance.
examples: No plan for Q4 yet — we'll play it by ear.
We played it by ear during the beta and it worked.
words.mission: Say where you can play it by ear, and where you cannot.

words.trap: Second sense of a known word: to sunset a product is to retire it — not the evening sky.
words.definition: to stop supporting a product or feature gradually, until it is switched off.
examples: We're sunsetting the v1 API in June.
Sunset the old plans before the pricing change.
words.mission: Name one feature that should be sunset, and when.

words.definition: to finish the small remaining tasks so that something is completely done.
examples: Two days to tie up loose ends, then we hand over.
She tied up the loose ends before her leave.
words.mission: List the loose ends of one project and tie up one today.

words.trap: Not 'clôture' as in a fence or a closing ceremony: closure is the feeling of having finished.
words.definition: the feeling that something has properly ended, so people can move on.
examples: A short retro gives the team closure.
Without a final demo there was no closure on the project.
words.mission: Plan one small ritual that gives a project closure.

words.definition: to stop using something gradually, in stages.
examples: We'll phase out the old dashboard over two months.
The legacy exports were phased out last year.
words.mission: Say what should be phased out, and over how long.

words.definition: public thanks or praise for a person, usually in a meeting or a message.
examples: Shout-out to Sara for the migration runbook.
A quick shout-out before we close: QA found the last bug.
words.mission: Give one shout-out in the team channel today.

words.trap: Two senses: to switch a machine off, and, for people, to stop thinking about work.
words.definition: to stop thinking about work and relax.
examples: After a launch, take a day and really switch off.
I can't switch off when the pager is next to me.
words.mission: Say what helps you switch off after a big release.

words.definition: the act of saying goodbye, especially at the end of a job or a project.
examples: We're doing a farewell lunch for Karim on Friday.
Her farewell email thanked the whole team.
words.mission: Plan one farewell moment for a colleague or a project.

words.trap: Not 'rester' (to stay) — for that say stay. A rest is a break. 'The rest' also means the others.
words.definition: a period of relaxing or sleeping after work or effort.
examples: Take a proper rest after the launch — you've earned it.
The team needs a rest before the next big push.
words.mission: Tell someone to take a rest — and mean the English sense.

words.definition: to return something to the person or team that owned it before.
examples: We hand the servers back to the client on Friday.
Hand back the badges and laptops before you leave.
words.mission: List what you will hand back at the end of one project.

words.trap: Informal and British; with a client, say thank you.
words.definition: an informal British way to say thank you or goodbye.
examples: Cheers for the quick review!
That's everything from me — cheers, all.
words.mission: End one chat message with 'cheers'.

words.trap: Say /waɪnd/ like 'find' — not like the wind that blows.
words.definition: to reduce activity gradually before stopping completely.
examples: The project winds down in March; two people stay on.
We're winding down support for the old version.
words.mission: Say what winds down first at the end of your project.

words.definition: work that was completed well, usually said when praising someone.
examples: Congratulations on a job well done.
The client's email was one line: 'a job well done'.
collocations: congratulations on a job well done
words.mission: Congratulate one person on a job well done, by name.

words.trap: Informal and British; in a report say pleased.
words.definition: very pleased (informal, British).
examples: I'm chuffed with how the launch went.
The team was chuffed to see the numbers.
words.mission: Say what you are chuffed about this month.

words.definition: said to encourage people to move on to the next, better thing after finishing something.
examples: That's the project closed — onwards and upwards!
Onwards and upwards: the next sprint starts Monday.
words.mission: Close one project with 'onwards and upwards'.

words.definition: to continue doing something.
examples: Carry on with the cleanup; I'll join after the call.
The team carried on as normal during the handover.
words.mission: Tell someone to carry on, and say with what.
